Because of the four *āsava* there is *oghā*;
thus, *oghā* consists of the four *āsava*.
What prevents the existence of the ālayavijñāna because of ignorance,
such that the ālaya possesses ignorance? Answer:
Due to ignorance, the dharmas of True Suchness (tathatā), which are inherently undefiled, become defiled.
This is not the same as the four latent tendencies (anuśaya) being simultaneously associated with the ālayavijñāna (ādānavijñāna).
Since the four latent tendencies would not exist if the ālayavijñāna were absent, the ālayavijñāna possesses these four latent tendencies.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"These three things cannot be found if they are separated from ignorance;
this ignorance cannot be found if it is separated from its basis."
To say that it exists and yet to say that its solitary activity is beginningless—
this might perhaps be so;
however, when investigated through reasoning:
The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states:
"That which does not contradict the meaning of the single Dharma-realm is called the ground of beginningless ignorance (*anādikālikāvidyā-āśraya*).
This ignorance, acting as a condition, is precisely the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) which, failing to comprehend the aspect of arising and ceasing, clings to it as a self."
At a later time, when one thoroughly realizes that it is merely a mind characterized by arising and ceasing, one immediately applies the antidote;
however, the ground of the abiding of ignorance is deluded because of a failure to understand the single principle of the Tathāgatagarbha, the Dharma-realm.
If one discusses the ability to counteract [delusion], it is by realizing that delusion is non-delusive;
only when understanding and contemplation accord with Suchness can one counteract consciousness that does not take the marks of arising and ceasing as its object.
Therefore, know that [your position] is not so.
The fifth pair both rely upon the sixth consciousness.
This is because the five sensory consciousnesses and the *ādāna-vijñāna* do not take the infinite merits as their object.
The sixth pair subsumes all afflictions, and the mind that encompasses them relies [upon the ālayavijñāna] without distinction.
The cognitive obstruction (jñeyāvaraṇa) relies solely upon the sixth consciousness;

the seventh [consciousness] relates to the afflictive obstruction (kleśāvaraṇa) and relies universally upon all consciousnesses, whereas the cognitive obstruction relies only upon the six consciousnesses,
because it fails to comprehend objects as they truly are.
Because the *ādānavijñāna* does not take external phenomena as its objective sphere, it is not that which is remedied by the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
These perfumed seeds both rely upon the *ālayavijñāna*.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
Defiled and wholesome [minds] attain continuity because they arise from their own seeds of perfuming.
Why is this? Because these two types of mind are sustained by the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna).
Delusion does not arise in isolation;
all these [defilements] depend upon the hidden, as they are contained within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
As the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states:
Regarding "birth-and-death" and "that which undergoes birth-and-death," these two dharmas both depend upon the *tathāgatagarbha*.
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* also says:
All phenomena are established based upon the ground of non-abiding.
Fifth, regarding the delusion that obstructs the principle and its phenomena,
there are two types of discrimination.
First, the object of obstruction differs in terms of principle and phenomenon.
Second, the obstructing delusion differs in terms of being with-outflow or without-outflow.
First, the object of obstruction differs in terms of principle and phenomenon.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the division of principle and phenomena according to seven meanings;
second, the specific differentiation of the distinct characteristics of principle and phenomena.
The first [set] consists of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*);
the fifth, sixth, and seventh consist of the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
That which is obstructed by these is phenomena (*vastu*), not principle (*tattva*).
The first, second, third, and fourth are obstacles to knowledge (jñeyāvaraṇa);
the fifth is the obstacle of afflictions (kleśāvaraṇa).
That which is obstructed by these is principle (li), not phenomena (shi).
The obstacles of the others pertain to both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*artha*).
Regarding the second section, which specifically distinguishes between phenomena and principle:
first phenomena, then principle.
Regarding the specific matters, the obstructions to dependent origination differ.
In the first and seventh [stages], external objects arise as obstructions to internal virtues;
the former obstruction obstructs the three practices, such as ethical discipline (*śīla*).
The seventh [hindrance] obstructs the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*).
The fifth and sixth [hindrances] obstruct the virtues that arise from relying upon meritorious deeds;
the fifth is capable of obstructing the nature of these afflictions (*kleśa*).
The sixth [affliction] is that which can obstruct wisdom.
Regarding the delusions concerning the principle of dependent origination,
because the fourth and fifth arise as delusions regarding the principle, they in turn obstruct the principle.
The first and second types of cognitive obscurations arise from being deluded regarding principles due to objective phenomena.
For example, when taking form as an object, one fails to understand that form exists and is devoid of a self;
or, when discussing what is right or wrong, one fails to understand that this is form and not a self, and so forth.
The first, second, and third are the principle of the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
The fourth and fifth are the principle of the suchness (*tathatā*) of existing phenomena.
The fourth corresponds to the reality of characteristics.
The fifth pair concerns the names and essences of the merits.
Within the section on characteristics, the first is the principle of the absence of a personal self (*pudgala-nairātmya*),
and the second is the principle of the absence of intrinsic nature (*dharmanairātmya*).
The third is the principle of the non-arising and lack of intrinsic nature of characteristics.
The others pertain to both the phenomenal and the noumenal aspects of the obstacles. Dependent origination and the obstacles can be understood through reflection.
The second [category] distinguishes between the obstructive outflows (*āsrava*) and the non-outflows (*anāsrava*).
First there is obstruction, followed by delusion.
Regarding obstruction, it refers to the first and a small portion of the second category of afflictions (*kleśa*).
The seventh is the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
These three [hindrances] depend upon and share the same objects as only contaminated consciousness (*sāsravacitta*).
The sixth cognitive hindrance depends upon and shares the same objects as only uncontaminated consciousness (*anāsravacitta*).
Fifth, the cognitive obstruction (jñeyāvaraṇa) universally relies upon and takes as its object both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) minds;
thus, it pervades both the tainted and the untainted.
Next, regarding those who are deluded:
The initial delusion and a portion of the second category of afflictions depend upon and share the same object as only impure (sāsrava) minds;
they are exclusively impure.
The others pertain to both.
When arising in ordinary beings, it is with outflows (*sāsrava*);
when the noble ones contemplate the mind and its mental factors, it is without outflows (*anāsrava*).
It is correct that [the views] such as the contemplation of the truth of suffering, which reckon suffering as having a self-nature and so forth, are indeed [afflictive obstructions].
The fifth, the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*), is exclusively impure (*sāsrava*);
the fourth, the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), is also [both pure and impure].
In the sixth stage, there arises the elimination of what precedes and follows.
Within this, that which arises first in the preceding stage is eliminated last.
As for that which arises in the first stage through conceptual discrimination:
The cognitive obstruction within the second [level] and the cognitive obstruction in the third—
these two arise as grounds for one another,
or because one calculates that natures possess distinct characteristics.
Alternatively, if one calculates that there is an intrinsic nature due to the existence of distinct characteristics,
while all others are deluded, this is the obstruction of the ground.
Based on arising from delusion, it is described as "origination."
Regarding the second point, the sequence of treatment and abandonment:
first, one counteracts the cognitive obstacles by means of the wisdom that realizes and abandons delusion;
subsequently, one gives rise to practice to eliminate the afflictive obstacles.
In the remaining six sections, in all cases, afflictions are severed first and the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are eliminated afterward.
What is the intention behind this?
It is because, in the initial [section], one first understands and subsequently practices.
First, one contemplates and eliminates the cognitive hindrance of delusion;
next, based on that contemplation, one gives rise to practice to eliminate the afflictive hindrance.
In the second, third, and fourth stages, as the clarity of principle becomes progressively deeper, the hindrances become correspondingly more subtle.
First one awakens to shallow principles,
then one awakens to profound principles;
first, with inferior wisdom, one abandons the coarse.
Next, superior wisdom eliminates the subtle [defilements].
The fifth [verse] reveals the essence and the arising of its virtues;
thus, it first removes the cognitive hindrances that obscure the principle to manifest the essential nature.
Based on the essence, the arising of qualities involves the removal of the cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa) as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
however, at the sixth [stage], one must first remove the nature of the afflictive obstructions (kleśāvaraṇa),
yet the arising of the antidote constitutes the cognitive obstruction.
Because the obstacle to knowledge is superior and the obstacle of afflictions is inferior,
the obstacle of afflictions is mentioned first and the obstacle to knowledge second.
According to the seventh principle, although there is in reality no sequence of priority and posteriority, they are spoken of as having such a sequence.
The subsequently attained wisdom arises after the wisdom of realization;
the former wisdom is the cause,
and the latter wisdom is the fruit.
If this is so, it is also possible to first speak of the afflictive hindrance (kleśāvaraṇa) and then the cognitive hindrance (jñeyāvaraṇa).
The seventh stage clarifies the limits of the realization of exhaustion;
this applies to both the initial pairing and the second reversal.
The afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are all completely severed prior to the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).

The cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are severed from the initial moment of the stage of the spiritual lineage up until the completion of the mind of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryā*).
The third type of cognitive hindrance is severed from the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) onwards.
Regarding ultimate wisdom,
as well as regarding the nature of the afflictive hindrances,
these are abandoned from the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) onwards.
Regarding the obstacles to merit and knowledge, as well as the seventh pair [of obstacles], both are severed at the initial moment of the first stage (*bhūmi*).

When they reach the point of extinction at the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*), their seeds are entirely eliminated and arise as the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). This constitutes the realization.
Regarding the distinctions between the methods for treating and severing [afflictions] according to reality, they are as explained in the section on "Severing the Bonds.
Eighth is the analysis of the inclusion of hindrances,
which first comprises the three hindrances.
The hindrance of the skin is subsumed under the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Both the flesh and the heart are subsumed under both hindrances;
those who are deluded regarding the principle of emptiness are considered the "flesh."
It is because beginningless ignorance constitutes the mind that it is so. If one were to subsume it under the three types of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), they are:
the latent tendency that destroys its companions, the latent tendency that is feeble, and the latent tendency that is attenuated.
These three, in terms of their meaning, also generally constitute both obstacles.
If they are contrasted with the [wisdom] that has existed from time immemorial, they are subsumed under the obstacle to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
If they are contrasted with the all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*), they are judged to be subsumed under the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

Furthermore, it should be understood that the hindrance of meditative concentration (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*) is subsumed under the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*), while the hindrance to liberation (*vimokṣāvaraṇa*) and the hindrance to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are both subsumed under these two.
Regarding the three outflows (*āsrava*):
That is to say, the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*),
and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) are all subsumed under the first two obstacles;
when three or four are added [to these], they constitute the full set.
The icchantika’s slander of the Dharma and the outsider’s attachment to a self—
these two views are categorized as cognitive obscurations (jñeyāvaraṇa) when contrasted with the paths of seeing and cultivation;
however, when contrasted with the conventional and the ultimate, they are subsumed under the afflictive obscurations (kleśāvaraṇa).
The fear of suffering in śrāvakas and the renunciation of the pratyekabuddhas are both subsumed under the two obstacles; with respect to the former,
it is subsumed under the obstacle of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
because they do not penetrate the principle of the absence of intrinsic nature.
Regarding the subsequent hindrances of afflictions, they are subsumed under the four floods (*ogha*). Among these,
the flood of views (*dṛṣṭy-ogha*) is subsumed under the hindrance of knowledge at its initial stage.

The outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) are subsumed under the two obstacles corresponding to the first pair [of afflictions].

Regarding the four graspings (*catvāry upādānāni*): the two graspings consisting of views (*dṛṣṭi-upādāna*) are both subsumed under the obstacle to knowledge (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) corresponding to the first pair [of afflictions].
The grasping for sensual desire (*kāma-upādāna*) and the grasping for the doctrine of self (*ātma-vāda-upādāna*) are both subsumed under the first two of the two obstacles.
As for the four yokes (*yoga*),
they are the yoke of sensual desire, the yoke of existence, the yoke of ignorance, and the yoke of views, as explained in the section on the four floods (*ogha*).
The four bonds—greed, hatred, views, and delusions—are explained as the four graspings. Regarding the four obstructions:
false reflection, false intention, doubt regarding the Dharma, and attachment to conceptualization;
among these, false intention is subsumed under the cognitive obstruction (jñeyāvaraṇa) from the very beginning.
The single category of doubt is subsumed under the seventh cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*);
it should be understood that the remaining [hindrances] are subsumed under both [the afflictive and cognitive hindrances].
[The number of categories] increases from four to five.
The five lower fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni) are subsumed under the first two heavy obstacles;

the three fetters are subsumed under the obstacle of cognition (jñeyāvaraṇa), namely: the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), attachment to precepts and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa), and doubt (vicikitsā).
Two fetters are subsumed under the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*),
namely greed and hatred.
The five higher-tier fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) are exclusively subsumed under the afflictive hindrance.
That is to say, restlessness, pride, ignorance, the defilement of the form realm,

and the defilement of the formless realm are subsumed under the five hindrances and the four hindrances as afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). The hindrance of doubt is subsumed under the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
If categorized according to their subsequent retribution,
they are subsumed under the afflictions of the five dwelling-grounds (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*) and the three dwelling-grounds (*tri-vāsabhūmi*).
It should be understood that views and ignorance are collectively subsumed under both obstacles (*dvividha-āvaraṇa*).
The five mental calamities refer to doubting the Buddha, doubting the Dharma, doubting the Saṅgha, doubting the precepts, and doubting the teachings.
These are all subsumed under the first pair of obstacles.
Increasing from five to six,
they are all subsumed under the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).
The first, the defilement associated with attachment (*saṃprayukta-kleśa*), subsumes the first two obstacles.
The defilement associated with non-interruption;
the defilement associated with the analytical knowledge of discrimination;
and the fundamental karmic defilements of the manifested form and mind that are dissociated from consciousness.
These are all subsumed under the affliction-obstructions (kleśāvaraṇa) of the latter five categories and the seventh category;
if the six stains are subsumed, they are all subsumed under the affliction-obstruction of the first category:
namely, vexation (nirveda), deception (māyā), arrogance (mada), injury (vihiṃsā), resentment (upanāha), and guile (śāṭhya).
Increasing from six to seven, the seven *anuśayas* (latent tendencies) are subsumed within the first two categories of the heavy obstacles (*guru-āvaraṇa*). These seven are:
greed (*rāga*), pride (*māna*), ignorance (*avidyā*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), attachment (*anunaya*), hatred (*pratigha*), and views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Increasing from seven to eight:
that is, the eight unwholesome thoughts are all subsumed under the initial obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
These are: desire, ill will, harm, kinship, governance of the realm, immortality, and contempt for one's clan.
Increasing from eight to nine:
the nine kinds of impurity are the most heavy latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the three poisons in the state of intense mental activity (*adhimātra-citta*).
These three poisons are to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
These are all subsumed under the first [category], the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
The ignorance-ground (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) to be abandoned through the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya*), as well as the defilements of the impure ground and the defilements of the pure ground,
are all subsumed under the latter fivefold two-fold hindrances (*dvividhāvaraṇa*).
And the seventh is subsumed under the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*),
not the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
The nine fetters (*saṃyojana*) are all subsumed under the first two hindrances.
Increasing from nine to ten refers to the ten obstacles (*daśāvaraṇa*).
With the exception of the second and third, all are subsumed under the two obstacles corresponding to the fifth and sixth [categories].
Furthermore, the seventh is subsumed under the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and the fourth is subsumed under the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
The second and third are the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the afflictions corresponding to the fourth [hindrance].
If the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) are subsumed,
lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), along with torpor (*middha*) and so forth, pertain to both of the first two obstacles;
the remaining six are all subsumed within the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Restlessness, regret, stinginess, envy, anger, and concealment—
if these ten afflictions (*kleśa*) are subsumed,

then the delusions of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) are all included within the first category of the heavy cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Greed, pride, hatred, and ignorance—
these four are subsumed within the first two categories of the heavy obstacles; when increased by ten or eleven,
they include the subtle obstacle of knowledge.
These are subsumed under the two obstacles (āvaraṇa) of the seventh stage.
They increase from eleven to thirteen, namely:

laziness, agitation, regret, lack of respect, inability to properly benefit sentient beings, affliction of the soft and pure mind, lack of skillful means, views regarding the ultimate and the conventional, views regarding the characteristics of practice, not seeing the characteristic of cessation, not seeing the characteristic of arising, gross pervasiveness, and extreme subtlety.
The subtle hindrance of wisdom and the hindrance of not perceiving the characteristic of arising— these two hindrances are both subsumed under the hindrance of wisdom within the seventh category.
The hindrance of indolence is subsumed under the hindrances of affliction within the first, second, third, and fourth categories.
The remainder are all subsumed under the cognitive obscuration within the fourth [category], as well as the two obscurations—the fifth and sixth—and the afflictive obscuration within the seventh;
they consist of thirteen to twenty-two types of ignorance.
The two types of ignorance—namely, pervasive ignorance and subtle honey-like ignorance—are subsumed under the seventh category, the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
The ignorance regarding karma that leads to the miserable realms is subsumed under the first three categories and the two obscurations.
The fourth is the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
All others are subsumed under the fourth, the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), as well as the sixth, which comprises both hindrances, and the seventh, the afflictive hindrance.
These increase from twenty-two up to thirty, and even to eighty-four thousand.
The nature and characteristics may be understood by analogy.
There are six sections of analysis regarding the meaning of "not abiding in the path.
The first is titled: "Name."
Second, the analysis of the essence of realization, which establishes the meaning of non-abiding;
third, the analysis of obstacles;
and fourth, the analysis of the objective spheres of abiding.
Fifth, the distinction of benefits;
sixth, the classification of stages.
Regarding the first name:
"Not" (bu) means "non-existence" (wu).
"Not" (bu) means "not doing so" (bù).
"Abiding" (zhù) refers to "attachment" (zhù).
The term "abiding" (sthiti) means "to exist.
As for the "path" (mārga), it is called the path because it consists of skillful practice in two ways that removes difficulties and is free from obstructions;
alternatively, it is designated as the path because it is that which is traversed.
Regarding the second point, the analysis of the nature of realization as the meaning of non-abiding,
there are two types. The first clarifies non-abiding from the perspective of contemplation.
Second, regarding non-abiding through the practice of clarity:
as for the first contemplation,
the objective sphere of focus has no distinct entity upon which one could abide.
Because birth-and-death is itself nirvana and nirvana is itself birth-and-death,
and because there is no nirvana apart from birth-and-death, one does not give rise to the thought of seeking realization through attainment.
Because there is no birth-and-death apart from nirvana, one does not give rise to the thought of preserving existence while abandoning [samsara].
Therefore, it is called "non-abiding.
To clarify the meaning of non-abiding in terms of practice:
by means of wisdom, one causes compassion to abide without defilement regarding existence and non-existence.
Because of compassion, wisdom does not abide by grasping at anything within the non-existent;
therefore, it is called "non-abiding.
As for the third pair, the analysis of obstacles:
There are two aspects of discernment (*vibhāga*): first, contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), and second, practice (*caryā*).
This is stated with reference to the initial cultivation of contemplation.
If one contemplates existence and non-existence in terms of their presence or absence, one sees that the nature of existence is devoid of intrinsic nature;
and by contemplating non-existence as existence, one sees it is devoid of annihilationism.
If one considers birth and death,
birth and death are themselves nirvana, which is to be free from the mind that seeks to abandon birth and death;
nirvana is itself birth and death, which is to be free from the mind that seeks to grasp and realize nirvana.
This concludes the explanation of the contemplation.
One observes existence as non-existent and observes non-existence as non-non-existent, thereby distancing the mind from both existence and non-existence;
for that which is neither existent nor non-existent is the objective realm of contemplation.
If one considers it in terms of nirvana:
observing that birth-and-death (saṃsāra) is without birth-and-death is the mind of nirvana that is detached from nirvana;
observing that nirvana is without nirvana is the mind of nirvana that is detached from birth-and-death.
Regarding the practitioner:
when first practicing these teachings, one distances oneself from the extremes of nihilism and eternalism.
Because great compassion follows after existence, one distances oneself from the attachment to nihilism.
By observing through wisdom that things are non-existent, one abandons the view of eternalism;
ultimately, this results in a mind that dwells in seclusion from speech.
By knowing birth and death as they truly are through wisdom, one abandons the dwelling in pleasure.
Through great compassion, one does not begrudge the attainment of nirvana and remains distant from its premature realization.
Furthermore, through wisdom, one abandons the ordinary person’s mind that delights in dwelling within saṃsāra;
and through great compassion, one remains distant from the mind of the two vehicles that dwells in nirvana. Fourth, as for the sphere in which one abides:
Compassion does not abide in non-abiding existence;
wisdom does not abide in existence but abides in non-existence. If one speaks of contemplation, it does not abide in the two principles of existence and non-existence.
One abides in the single flavor of suchness, which is neither existent nor non-existent.
A question is asked:
"Since there are already objective spheres (viṣaya), [how can this be so?]"
Perversity is established as non-abiding;
when understood, it is called the Way.
Although compassion has an object, [it is not fixed].
Through wisdom, compassion remains unstained by existence;
though wisdom possesses an object,
through compassion, wisdom does not abide in non-existence.
The observer does not abide in either of these two types.
Fifth, regarding the distinction of the benefit conferred:
to speak of the differentiation of their characteristics—
Great compassion benefits others;
wisdom benefits oneself.
If we speak in terms of what they encompass, regarding both ordinary beings and sages:
Each [of these] possesses two meanings, and great compassion has two skillful means:
first, to conform to birth-and-death in order to gather in ordinary beings;
second, not to hastily realize nirvana in order to gather in the noble ones.
Wisdom has two skillful means:
first, knowing birth-and-death as it truly is—being without intrinsic nature—which subsumes the noble ones;
second, penetrating the ultimate bliss of nirvāṇa—which subsumes ordinary beings.
Furthermore, these four may all be understood to encompass both ordinary persons and noble ones.
Regarding the sixth point, the differentiation of stages (*bhūmi*),
there are two types of differentiation.
Prior to the first stage, within the gateway of the ten faiths,
compassion is weak and thin, and one lacks joy in and equanimity toward the Mahāyāna;
for this reason, the meaning of non-abiding is not yet clear.
Within the ten gates of understanding (*daśa-avabodha-mukha*), it is precisely here that non-abiding is clarified;
within this stage, two factors are fully present:
first, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) as the primary guide.
Second is the predominance of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
If one proceeds from the tenth stage onward, great compassion becomes fulfilled;
that is to say, within this stage, the contemplation of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) brings great compassion to fulfillment.

Having completed the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), up until the first stage (*bhūmi*), one fulfills great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) characterized by signlessness (*animitta*), non-arising (*anutpāda*), and the nature of being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Upon entering the stages, on the third and fourth stages, one is designated merely as "guarding against afflictions" (*kleśa-rakṣā*) and "guarding against the Lesser Vehicle" (*hīnayāna-rakṣā*).
The reason for this is that the third stage constitutes the skillful means of illumination for encompassing the virtues of practice,
due to the presence of both the mind of aspiration and the mind of revulsion.
The essence of the practice on the fourth stage consists in eliminating the two obstacles;
thus, it is said that one protects against affliction and protects against the Lesser Vehicle.
It is on the fifth and sixth stages that one clearly manifests non-abiding.
One practices through clarity;
within the phenomena to be known, one benefits sentient beings by performing the contemplation of the fourteen truths of purification.
Within diligent skillful means, one contemplates conditioned phenomena as false, deceptive, and so forth, thereby accomplishing great compassion.
From the sixth stage onward, both types of clear understanding (*vidyā*) are attained.
Regarding the contemplation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one clearly realizes through contemplation that there is no abiding.
Within the contemplation of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in both reverse and forward order.
One practices while not dwelling [in signs].

According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, there are nine causes and conditions.

The first three sets [of practices] serve to generate liberation, resolve delusion, gather the mind in one-pointed concentration, abandon the extremes of eternalism and nihilism, maintain the precepts, distance oneself from karma, attain right knowledge, and eliminate false views.

Within the first three [stages],

If a person gives rise to doubt regarding the meaning,"
First, it is for the purpose of enabling the attainment of definitive knowledge;
second, it is for establishing the Vinaya,

The treatise states:
"The Vinaya was established separately in order to counteract the two extremes of enjoyment.
Furthermore, the treatise states:
Because the Buddha prohibited the enjoyment of things that involve faults, he established the Vinaya as an antidote against the extreme of indulgence in pleasure;

Because the Buddha rejoices in faultless enjoyment, he establishes the Vinaya as an antidote to the extreme of asceticism.
This clarifies that practicing in accordance with the Dharma and accomplishing wholesome karma of body and speech is what the Buddha rejoices in and praises.

As the treatise states:

The treatise says:
"Because it is for the sake of training based on the precepts and based on the mind, the Vinaya is established separately. Why is this?"

Third, the establishment of the Abhidharma:

Why is this? Because it is able to discern the non-erroneous meaning.

As explained extensively therein,

The Prātimokṣa precepts are the direct antidote to the seven unwholesome paths of action of body and speech that constitute the breaking of discipline, as well as the intention associated with those actions;
whereas the Bodhisattva precepts additionally serve as an antidote to the mental ground of right action and intention.
If one discusses the fundamental antidote for the precepts of guarding the sense faculties,

this is because their essence consists of mindfulness and wisdom.
Regarding the second point, the two paths of meditative concentration (dhyāna-mārga) that are common to both:
first, their commonality is established;
next, their similarities and differences are distinguished based on the three types of restraint (saṃvara).
The first [type] is that which is associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahagata*), sharing the same antidote as concentration and having the same fruit; therefore,
the *Samyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states:
The applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) sever the afflictions by means of grasping the full range of objects and by means of abbreviated objects;
the same applies to the paths associated with them.
Secondly, regarding the distinction between similarities and differences among the three types of restraint:
if one discusses the restraint of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃvara*) in relation to the nine grades of afflictions of breaking precepts in the desire realm,
the restraint of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) may or may not serve as an antidote.
The fundamental dhyāna restraint does not sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Therefore, the *Samyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states:
"The pure fundamental first dhyāna is likewise bound by the same fetter and cannot sever the afflictions."
The restraints at the limits of the second, third, and fourth dhyānas are all capable of severing the afflictions of the lower stages;

Thus, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states:
Although those born in the form and formless realms temporarily distance themselves from transgressing the precepts,
they cannot escape being contrary to the practice of ethical discipline.
The untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara) is present throughout all six stages.
The preparatory (anāgamya), intermediate (dhyānāntara), and the four fundamental dhyānas—
these six stages consist of the restraint of abandonment (prahāṇasaṃvara) for the preparatory dhyāna,

However, the untainted precepts of the future dhyāna stage share the same function as the Path;
they are able to sever the arising of unwholesome conduct that violates the precepts within the desire realm,
and they are also able to sever all afflictions of the two upper realms.
As for the remaining stages, their functional power is such that they can sever [defilements] of the three realms.

However, since those of the lower stages have already been abandoned, there is nothing left to counteract; thus, when one correctly applies effort, one severs only the [defilements] of one's own stage and the higher stages.
Question:
Why is there no establishment of restraint (*saṃvara*) in the formless realm? Answer:
The Vinaya discipline is established based on the *Tattvasiddhi*,
because it clarifies the remedies for the improper violation of precepts;
furthermore, this discipline is of the nature of form (*rūpa*).
Because the formless [realms] lack form.
Question:
The restraint of dhyāna is produced by the four great elements of its respective stage.
That stage lacks the [gross] great elements;
thus, it might lack the formal restraint (saṃvara).
However, the untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara) is produced by the four great elements that accompany the body.
When one's body is in the two lower realms,
one can give rise to untainted [states] based on the three lower formless attainments.
For what reason is there no untainted restraint (śīla) within that same assemblage?
Answer: Because the mind does not revolve around form, it shatters the appearance of form.
As for the seventh successive discrimination:
There are four kinds of analysis:
first, clarifying the sequence through the breadth or brevity of the expressed meaning;
second, the sequence of gathering benefits.
Third, the sequence of the exposition;
fourth, the sequence of the compilation.
Regarding the clarification of the sequence of the breadth and brevity of the expressed meaning:
As stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*:
"Furthermore, the Sūtras are established for the sake of teaching two kinds of training;
the Vinaya is separately established for the sake of relying upon the training in ethics and the training in mind."
The Abhidharma is established for the purpose of accomplishing the training in wisdom.
As for the sequence of its inclusion and benefit,
it is as explained in the previous section on distinctions.
Regarding the sequence of the teaching:
according to the *Lalitavistara Sūtra*,
the Buddha first taught the *Dharmacakra-pravartana Sūtra* in Vārāṇasī.
From this point onward, the sūtras are finally expounded.
According to the Mahāyāna,
on the second seventh-day period, the Lotus Sūtra was preached.
After twenty-one days, he preached the *Sūtra of the Great Assembly*;
after forty-nine days, he preached the *Sūtra*.
These various accounts of preceding and succeeding events are beyond the scope of what can be reconciled through mere seeing and hearing.
The reason for this sequence is that the precept against unchaste conduct was established by Kalandaka-putra;
first the Vinaya-piṭaka was expounded,
and later, at the side of the Monkey Tank in Vaiśālī, they were all assembled together in the lecture hall.
The Buddha, having perceived the beginning and end of the causal conditions concerning the Vajjis,
taught the five fears to the bhikṣus; namely,
those ranging from taking life to drinking intoxicants.
Regarding the sequence of the initial compilation of the Abhidharma,
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, he remained for seven days before finally entering his coffin and outer casket."
When the Licchavis and others had finished cremating the Tathāgata,
the eight kings divided the relics for the purpose of making offerings.
Therefore, Kāśyapa said to Ānanda:
The lay followers have repaid the Buddha’s kindness;
we, too, should now repay his kindness by assembling one thousand arhats in Rājagṛha to compile the Dharma-piṭaka.
First, he commanded Ānanda to recite the Sūtras;
next, he requested Upāli to recite the Vinaya Piṭaka;
and the Arhats further directed Ānanda to recite the Abhidharma Piṭaka.
The *Lalitavistara Sūtra* also speaks in this manner.
According to the *Aśokarāja-avadāna*,
he first commanded Ānanda to recite the sūtras in verse.
Kāśyapa himself versified the Abhidharma,
and later Upāli versified the Vinaya.
According to the *Five-Part Vinaya* (Pañcavargika-vinaya), it says:
First, Upāli was instructed to versify the Vinaya-piṭaka;
next, Ānanda was instructed to versify the Sūtra-piṭaka;
and finally, Ānanda was instructed to versify the Abhidharma-piṭaka.
Eighth, regarding the detailed and abbreviated classifications:
some say there is one;
that is, the teachings of the Tripiṭaka, when contrasted with the four types of external treatises (bāhyaka-śāstra), are collectively termed internal treatises (adhyātma-śāstra).
Alternatively, it is said that there are two [types]. As stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
these three become two kinds due to the distinction between the lower and higher vehicles.
That is to say, the Śrāvaka-piṭaka and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka;
this constitutes one pair, distinguished as the two categories of Great and Small Vehicles.
Alternatively, three types are taught.
Summarized by way of three categories, that which expresses [the meaning] constitutes the Three Piṭakas;
alternatively, four types are taught,
as Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna each have their own specific expressions and intents.
Some say there are six kinds,
with three each for the Great and Small [Vehicles].
Others say there are eight kinds.
To both the large and small [collections], the *Kṣudrakapiṭaka* (Miscellaneous Collection) is added.
Regarding this *Kṣudrakapiṭaka*, the *Vibhaṅgaguṇa-sūtra* states:
That which is called the *Kṣudrakapiṭaka* (Miscellaneous Collection) consists of that spoken by the Buddha, that spoken by his disciples, or that spoken by various devas.
There are not a few accounts concerning past lives (*pūrvajanman*), the conditions of karma, and the births of Bodhisattvas throughout the three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
The Dharma is likewise; therefore, it is called the *Kṣudrakapiṭaka*.
Question:
Why is the *Kṣudrakapiṭaka* established outside of the Three Piṭakas?
Question: For what reason is a "Miscellaneous Section" (*kṣudraka*) not established outside of the twelve divisions [of the scriptures]?
Answer: The teachings of the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*) correspond to the three types of practice (*trividha-caryā*) that they expound.
The meaning of practice and abiding does not rely on anything else;
for the teachings that express [the Dharma] do not encompass all phenomena exhaustively,
and thus one desires to encompass exhaustively those other things not yet explained.
The twelve divisions of the sūtras encompass the profound meaning with broad and thorough exposition, leaving nothing unsaid;
therefore, no separate "miscellaneous" division is established. Ninth, regarding the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles and the existence or non-existence [of dharmas]:
What is meant by "non-existent"?
The teachings of the Tripitaka reside within the Hīnayāna and do not exist within the Mahāyāna;
that which is called the Mahāyāna Piṭaka does not exist [in the former].
Furthermore, it is called the One Vehicle because it does not speak of three;
as a sutra says:
"One must not associate with those who study the Tripitaka."
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Kāśyapa and Ānanda compiled the Tripiṭaka at Rājagṛha as the Śrāvaka-piṭaka;
Mañjuśrī and Ānanda compiled the Mahāyāna at Mount Cakravāḍa as the Bodhisattva-piṭaka."
Question:
What is it that the Tripitaka elucidates? It is the three types of practice.
Why is this present in the Hīnayāna but absent in the Mahāyāna?
Answer: The three types of conduct are practiced for the sake of self-benefit.
Those of the Hīnayāna school intend only for their own virtuous practice and do not include others.
Therefore, from the perspective of one's own practice alone,
when the distinct teaching (*biejiao*) is used to describe self-practice, it is termed the "Lesser Vehicle" (*hīnayāna*).
Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, however, both deliver themselves and deliver others.
Based on the distinction between the practices of the two vehicles, the two types of practice are specifically identified as the Mahāyāna, which constitutes the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
What constitutes this "Great" [Vehicle]?
It is the greatness of self-benefit.
In the Small and Middle [Vehicles] there is no benefit for others;
because they possess benefit for oneself, there is also the Tripiṭaka of the Mahāyāna.
Thus, the Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra says:
The Tathāgata has three modes of speech, namely:
the exposition of the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma.
The Saṃdhinirmocana and the Lalitavistara Sūtras also speak of the Mahāyāna Tripiṭaka.
Therefore, the Mahāyānasaṃgraha states:
"How many kinds of this Bodhisattvapiṭaka are there?
There are also three kinds."
That is to say, the Sūtra, Abhidharma, and Vinaya.
These three become two types due to the distinction between the Higher and Lower Vehicles;
namely, the Śrāvaka Piṭaka and the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.
Regarding the tenth section, the analysis of inclusion (*saṃgraha-vibhāga*),
there are three parts. First,
the analysis of inclusion by correlating the Three Piṭakas with the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*).
The inclusion [of the teachings] is determined by comparing the three collections (tripiṭaka) with one another, and by comparing the three [collections] with the two [vehicles].
Regarding the first, the determination of inclusion by comparing the three collections with the twelve divisions of the scriptures (dvādaśāṅga-buddhavacana), there are two [points].

First, the analysis according to the meaning of the categories (*artha*) explains how they encompass one another’s essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); however, this does not necessarily exhaust all logical principles.
Second, the analysis according to general logical principles (*yukti*) distinguishes how they encompass one another.
Regarding the first section, the correlation between the expressed meaning and the encompassing categories:
the Tripitaka, as the teaching that expresses [the meaning], encompasses twelve divisions (*dvādaśāṅga*) of the teachings that express it—
namely, the Sūtra, Geya, Gāthā, and Udāna— and four divisions.
Regarding the inclusion of the expressed meaning (*abhidheya-lakṣaṇa-saṃgraha*):
among the remaining six sections, excluding the Jātaka and Adbhutadharma,
the Śīla [Varga] is subsumed under Śīla.
Concentration subsumes concentration;
wisdom subsumes wisdom.
Regarding the mutual inclusion of these two according to the general principle:
If the *Kṣudrakapiṭaka* (Miscellaneous Collection) is categorized into the three piṭakas according to the three types of discourse,
then— excluding the *Sūtra*, *Jātaka*, *Vaidalya*, and *Adbhutadharma*—
the *Sūtra* is so designated because it proclaims the principles of the Four Noble Truths through its prose exposition.
The Jātaka-vastu concerns bodies received in the past;
the Itivṛttaka-vastu concerns the teachings spoken by past Buddhas,
namely, the principles of the two truths.

The *Adbhuta-dharma* (Marvels), the *Prātihārya* (Miracles), and the various celestial deities of the earth are not included [in the *Sūtra-piṭaka*] because they do not exclusively explain the three types of conduct (*tri-carita*). Alternatively,

if one excludes the *Jātaka* (Birth Stories) and *Vaidalya* (Past Deeds) and considers only those long prose narratives that explain the three types of conduct as being the *Sūtra-piṭaka*, then it is so.
If this is so, according to other schools, those that explain the three types of practitioners are subsumed under the Three Baskets (Tripiṭaka),
while those that do not explain the three types of practitioners are not so subsumed;
thus, one can understand how the twelvefold division is subsumed within the Three Baskets.
It is precisely as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:
the Sūtra Piṭaka does not exclusively clarify meditative concentration.
If that is so, the Sūtra Piṭaka comprehensively subsumes all twelve [divisions of the teachings].
The Vinaya Piṭaka comprises the twelve internal [sections] that expound upon ethical discipline (*śīla*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
the Abhidharma Piṭaka comprises the twelve internal [sections] that expound upon wisdom (*prajñā*).
Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
That is to say, the Sūtra-piṭaka is established separately because it teaches the three types of training;
the Vinaya-piṭaka is established separately to establish the training in higher ethics or the training of the mind;
and the Abhidharma-piṭaka is established separately to establish the training in higher wisdom.
This can be understood by means of the twelve divisions [of the scriptures] subsuming the three baskets (tripiṭaka).
Question:
What is the difference between the Sūtra-piṭaka within the three baskets and the Sūtra division within the twelve divisions?
Answer: There are three kinds of sūtras.
First, the sūtras within the Tripitaka.
Among the twenty-two divisions, it is specifically called *sūtra*;
among the thirty-two divisions, it is collectively called *sūtra*.
According to the *Vibhāṣā*:
Within the Tripitaka, the Sūtra-piṭaka only encompasses those portions of the twelve divisions of scripture that definitively explain general and specific meanings;

it does not encompass the other two piṭakas, nor those portions of the twelve divisions that definitively explain discipline (śīla) and wisdom (prajñā), nor the Miscellaneous Piṭaka (Kṣudraka-piṭaka).
Within the twelve divisions [of the scriptures], the general *sūtra* division comprehensively subsumes both the Tripiṭaka and the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka*.
It also subsumes the twelve divisions as they collectively expound the meaning of the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*).
Within the twelve divisions, the specific *sūtra* division subsumes the Tripiṭaka and the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka*.
The two types of verses and sūtras are not included;
all others are fully included. Why is this?
Because it is taught as a separate section by means of prose (gadya),
according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
the Sūtra Piṭaka comprehensively includes the other two Piṭakas.
The *Kṣudraka-piṭaka* (Miscellaneous Collection) is not included.
If one considers the twelve divisions of the scriptures, it includes only those portions that explain the three types of practice; all others are not included.
Furthermore, according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
the Sūtra Piṭaka is for the purpose of eliminating the doubts of others and for elucidating the unimpeded realm. If this is so,
it can be understood that the inclusion by meaning does not reside within the inclusion by characteristics.
Regarding the second point, the analysis of the inclusion [of the teachings] by comparing the three Piṭakas, there are three types:
first, inclusion by the majority;
second, inclusion by distinct categories.
Regarding the inclusion within the three characteristics,
as for "mostly included," the *Vibhāṣā* states:
In the Sūtras, there is both the analysis of ethical discipline and the analysis of wisdom;
in the Vinaya, there is both the analysis of the mind and the analysis of wisdom;
and in the Abhidharma, there is both the analysis of the mind and the analysis of ethical discipline.
What is the distinction between these three collections?
The answer is:
it is according to their predominant content.
In the Sūtras, the mental factors (citta-dharma) are predominantly taught;
in the Vinaya, the precepts (śīla-dharma) are predominantly taught;
and in the Abhidharma, the wisdom factors (prajñā-dharma) are predominantly taught.
This is the summary by way of majority.
As for the summary by way of distinct categories,
the Sūtras clarify the three trainings.
The Vinaya and Abhidharma are also like this.
Therefore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states:
"In the Sūtras, if the mind is analyzed, it is called 'Sūtra'."
If the analysis of ethical discipline (*śīla*) is called *vinaya*,
and the analysis of wisdom (*prajñā*) is called *abhidharma*,
then within the *abhidharma*, the analysis of ethical discipline is called *vinaya*.
If the mind of discrimination is called Sūtra,
and if the wisdom of discrimination is called Abhidharma,
then within the Vinaya, the wisdom of discrimination is likewise called Abhidharma.
If one distinguishes the precepts, they are called Vinaya;
if one distinguishes the mind, they are called Sūtra.
As for their mutual inclusion:
Within the Sūtra-piṭaka, even if it explains precepts or wisdom, it is all termed the Sūtra-piṭaka;
the same applies to the Vinaya and Abhidharma.
Third, regarding the analysis of the meaning of inclusion through the contrast between the Great and Small [Vehicles], there are two [points].
First, the distinct characteristics of the large and small mutually encompass one another;
second, the large governs the small.
Regarding the mutual encompassing of distinct characteristics:
In the teachings of the Hīnayāna, the four Āgamas and other such scriptures are called the Sūtra Piṭaka;
the five divisions of the Vinaya are called the Vinaya Piṭaka;
and the six *pāda* Abhidharma treatises expounded by the Buddha, along with various other scholastic commentaries, are called the Abhidharma Piṭaka.
Within the Mahāyāna Dharma, the *Avataṃsaka* and other such sūtras are called the Sūtra Piṭaka;
the pure Vinaya is called the Vinaya Piṭaka;
and the *Mūla-abhidharma*, which elucidates the ten kinds of supreme characteristics and so forth, is called the Mātṛkā Piṭaka.
Second, regarding the subsuming of the small by the great:
regardless of whether they belong to the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, all sūtras are included within the profound Vaipulya sūtras and are termed the Sūtra Piṭaka;
all precepts and disciplines practiced by Bodhisattvas are included within the Vinaya Piṭaka.
The Abhidharma of the Hīnayāna and all those commentaries that explain the meaning of this Piṭaka are entirely included within the Mātṛkā-piṭaka.
Regarding the meaning of the *piṇḍoddāna* (summary verses), the meaning of the *piṇḍoddāna* is analyzed by means of four gates.
First, the names;
second, the essential nature;
third, the detailed explanation according to the vehicles.
Fourth, the general classification.
Regarding the first name:
"pī" (chapter) is a synonym for "zhāng" (section) or "pǐn" (fascicle).
"Aggregate" (skandha) means a collection.
Regarding its second essential nature:
if considered in terms of that which expresses [it],...
Its essence consists of sound, name, flavor, and so forth;
if one refers to that which is expressed,
its nature consists of the three types of action (karma).
The third [section] provides a detailed explanation according to the distinct vehicles: first, the Śrāvakayāna is analyzed;
second, the Bodhisattvayāna is analyzed.
If the Śrāvaka-dharma were to be analyzed in detail, it would be fully contained within the Vinaya teachings;
for now, however, we shall briefly perform the confession.
First, regarding the categories (pārājika) and the clusters (saṃghāvaśeṣa), each category is further divided into fourfold classifications.
First, the names;
second, the essential nature;
third, the analysis of increase and decrease.
Regarding the first of the four sequential clarifications, there is a threefold analysis:
first, establishing the general name;
second, explaining the specific names.
Third, the explanation of how the name is obtained.
Regarding the first [of the three meanings], there are three senses.
The first sense is "uniformity" (samatā).
Second, their substance is equal;
third, they are equally ultimate.
Regarding "equal substance":
Furthermore, regarding the four grave offenses collectively termed *pārājika*,
those whose nature is uniform are all extremely evil;
three of them are identical in being ultimate transgressions rather than mere preliminary acts.
Second, regarding the explanation of the specific names:
*pārājika* refers to offenses that leave no remainder and are also called "extremely grave.
As for *saṃghāvaśeṣa*:
According to the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-śāstra*,
the term in the local language is *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
*Saṃgha* is translated as "the Saṃgha."
*Pācittiya* refers to the beginning,
meaning the *pācittiya-kamma* (formal act of concealment);
*sīsa* refers to the end.
This refers to the final *karmavācanā* for the removal of offenses.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vibhāṣā* states:
"The Saṃgha is called 'Saṃgha'."
"Vasi" means "remnant. Do not allow the use of what has been purified by means of a remnant.
Offenses are eliminated through the Saṃgha.
*Pāyattika* means "falling";
one falls into the various evil destinies.
*Pratideśanīya* means "that which can treat through the practice of repentance."
A minor offense is termed *duṣkṛta*.
Third, regarding the establishment of names:
the first and the fifth are named based on the essential nature of the offense itself.
The second [category] establishes its designation based on the nature of the object;
"saṃgha" is the object, and "residue" (śeṣa) is its nature.
The third [category] reveals its name by way of the offense incurred.
The fourth is designated according to the feeling that serves as the remedy.
Furthermore, the first and second may also be established by name according to their dharmas,
namely, the remaining dharmas and the non-remaining dharmas.
The remainder is as before.
Regarding the second essence:
Question.
Among the three aggregates of phenomena, which aggregate constitutes their essence?
Answer: According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
Form is neither form nor mind; its nature is [neither].
Question:
Could there be no fault in an assemblage of mind?
Answer: Because the mind has no capacity to counteract the restraint of the precepts,
the substance of the transgression to be countered is not established.
According to the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*,
if one considers it from the perspective of the fundamental courses of action (*mūlakarmapatha*), its essence consists of informative and non-informative form (*vijñapti-avijñaptirūpa*).
If explained according to both interpretations,
it generally refers to the mind;
as clarified in the Vinaya, it likewise generally refers to the mind.
For instance, regarding thoughts such as malice or killing, the *duṣkṛta* (offense) is established within the mental ground (*manobhūmi*).
Question:
Why does the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* state that the two categories of body and speech constitute its essence?
Answer: The Vinaya distinguishes offenses based on the fundamental preparatory acts (*prayoga*),
whereas the Śāstra treats them as following from the fundamental physical and vocal actions.
It is simply said that the two types of karma have [unwholesome] volition as their nature.
Question:
Is there also misdeed through expedient means on the mental level?
It should also be said that there is the precept of skillful means within the mental ground. Answer:
The skillful means of the precept is not itself the precept.
Question:
Should the preparatory effort for a transgression also be considered non-transgression?
Answer: No.
It is not a root offense.
Question:
Although it is not a root offense, its essence is nonetheless a transgression.
One might also argue that although it is not the root, its essence is nonetheless precept.
Answer: It constitutes a transgression because the nature of the offense is distinct from its accomplishment.
Skillful means is also itself a transgression,
because the goodness of the precepts is difficult to accomplish; thus,
the skillful means of these precepts is not the precepts themselves.
Question: Guarding against what is non-virtuous is called precept (*śīla*).
If one employs skillful means of body and speech with a virtuous mind and is able to distance oneself from unwholesome dharmas at that moment, why is this not called a precept?
If a thought of harm arises in the mental faculty (manobhūmi), but one restrains it, that wholesome mental state is not called a transgression.
Answer: There are indeed precepts that do not prevent non-virtue.
Just as with non-action (*avijñapti*) and so forth,
that which naturally prevents wrongdoing is not itself called "precept" (*śīla*);
rather, it is like the preparatory effort for the arising of precepts from the mental ground (*manobhūmi*).
How can this be taken as an analogy?
Regarding the third point on increase and decrease:
for what reason does it not increase to six nor decrease to four?
This is so because it is intended for the specific needs of transformation in one particular region.
Some say this refers to the five destinies,
but that is not necessarily the case.
Should the seven groups [of offenses] also correspond to the seven paths?
Regarding the fourth point, the determination of sequence:
the treatise states that the establishment of the precepts does not necessarily follow a fixed chronological order.
However, the compilers of the canon prioritized the more significant over the minor and recorded them in this order.
Since the first chapter concerns that which can cure— the very root of practice—
and because that which is to be cured is extremely grave, it is discussed first.
The second is the net (*jāla*),
which is discussed next because it governs the *saṃgha*.
The third is deportment (*īryāpatha*).
Because it is recited three times before another person,
the fourth practice, the confession of transgressions (*deśanā*),
is discussed next. Because it is recited once before another person to eliminate the fault of being out of harmony with others, it is discussed next.
The fifth is the mind of respectful inquiry.
Because it is a practice of reverence, it is placed as the fifth among the excellent discourses.
Each of these possesses five meanings; they are discussed as five in order to distinguish them from one another.
Therefore, the Vinaya says:
"Burned away until nothing remains. Second, the meaning of the aggregate (*skandha*) is analyzed through five gates;
the first is its name.
Second, the two natures;
third, whether the sthūlātyaya offenses are included within the categories [of the Vinaya] or not;
fourth, the position of the sthūlātyaya offenses as being in the third or the sixth [categories].
The fifth section harmonizes the *skandhas* and *vargas*.
Regarding the first name,
there are seven distinct categories within the *skandha*.
The five categories constitute five [sections];
further adding the *sthūlātyaya*,
the third category is divided into two.
That is to say, thirty-nine and forty;
these are as explained in the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
The remaining names are as previously stated.
Regarding the explanation of *sthūlātyaya*:
"obstructing" (*āvaraṇa*) means to block or hinder;
it is named according to its functional effect.
Question:
For what reason is the third category among the five groups of offenses divided into two clusters? Answer:
This is due to the distinction between relinquishing and not relinquishing. Question:
Within the second category, there is the distinction between admonishing and not admonishing.
This should also be divided into two parts. Answer:
At thirty-nine or forty years of age, one must first relinquish [the precepts] before performing the confession.
Because one confesses without abandoning [the offense],
they are divided into two.
Within the second category, there is not a single dharma that requires formal admonition before it can be confessed.
There is not a single dharma that does not require admonition for repentance.
Since the act of repentance is uniform and no further distinct methods are added,
they are combined into one.
Question:
Since those who have abandoned [the precepts] and those who have not are divided into two groups,
they should likewise be divided into two sections.
Answer: Regarding the meaning of "falling" (*patati*), they are equal in their scope;
all three explanations concerning the external [objects] resolve the meaning through five gates.
Therefore, they were combined into one.
Now, because the seventh section explains the meaning through the categories of "abandoning" and "not abandoning," it is divided into two.
Second, the essential nature (*svabhāva*).
If one wishes to analyze it as previously stated,
the third [section] clarifies whether a *sthūlātyaya* offense belongs to the category of transgressions or not.
Question:
For what reason is *sthūlātyaya* not established within this section?
There are two ways to distinguish this:
first, according to the traditional ancient interpretation.
Second, the detailed explanation of the principles.
Regarding the first, the establishment of the chapters possesses three meanings:
first, identity of name; second, identity of gravity.
The three are identical in their ultimate nature.
That which possesses these three is established;
that which does not possess these three is not established.

Although *sthūlātyaya* is a name shared with other offenses, it does not possess both characteristics [of being a grave offense and requiring a large assembly for confession]. For instance, offenses such as causing a schism in the Sangha require extinction through banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*), while those involving four *kārsāpaṇa* or more must be confessed before a large assembly.
Those involving three *kārsāpaṇa* or less, as well as heavy offenses belonging to the second category (*dvitīyāpatti*), are to be confessed within a small assembly.
In the case of minor offenses, the counterpart is the hand.
For example, if one’s original intent in breaking the Sangha is to take four *kārsāpaṇas* or the like, this constitutes the culmination; taking five is the preliminary effort (*upakrama*).
In such cases, the offense is a *sthūlātyaya*, which is the preliminary effort.
For this reason, it is not established as a separate category.
If that is so, since the fifth category encompasses both light and heavy offenses, as well as preparatory and consummated acts,
why is it established as a distinct category?
Answer: For a śrāmaṇera, the offense of extinction (nirodha) is a duṣkṛta, as he is not a fully ordained monk;
therefore, we do not discuss the preliminary effort (prayoga) separately, but speak directly of the final consummation (niṣṭhā).
Because the mental intent (*cetanā*) in all these cases is of one and the same degree, they are established as *sthūlātyaya*.
Since this excludes the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) and takes only the consummation (*niṣṭhā*),
and because it applies to both light and heavy offenses, [the term *duṣkṛta*] is not established here.
The second type involves following the heavy with the heavy,
such as the *nihsargika-pāyattika* offenses;
it also involves following the light with the heavy.
As in the case of taking four coins and so forth,
because they are subsumed under the five categories (*pañcāpatti*) by way of their fundamental basis through skillful means, they are not established separately;
yet within the classification of the groupings, the heavy offenses are differentiated.
Because there are differences in gravity and distinctions between the preparatory (*upāya*) and the fundamental (*mūla*),
the category of *sthūlātyaya* was established in addition to the five groups (*pañcāpatti-skandha*).
Fourth, it clarifies why *sthūlātyaya* is placed between the third and sixth [categories].
There are two types of analysis:
first, that which relies on traditional ancient exegesis;
second, that which analyzes according to principle.
Regarding the first:
if categorized according to precepts and the rules of dignified conduct (*airyāpathika*),
the first two are the precepts.
The latter four are matters of deportment (*airyāpathika*).
*Thullaccaya* is the first two stages of the preliminary effort (*prayoga*).
Furthermore, because it belongs to the category of residual offenses (*śeṣa*), it is placed in the third position.
If the factors of the mixed category are to be evenly distributed,
those that are weightiest within the even set are established as the first group,
and those that are lightest are established as the fifth group.
Among the miscellaneous offenses, those that are grave are established as *sthūlātyaya*,
while those that are light are established as the seventh [offense].
Because they are of a mixed nature, "evil speech" is established as the sixth.
The second case is as stated in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*:
wearing robes of the color of pure birds constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Is it not the case that this [category] which excludes [the others] is indeed *airyāpathika* (pertaining to deportment)?
If, according to this principle, one wishes to clarify that *sthūlātyaya* belongs to the category of the precepts (*śīla-skandha*), it is placed in the third [position];
if one wishes to clarify that *sthūlātyaya* further belongs to the category of deportment, it is established in the fifth [position].
Regarding the fifth stage, the "Section on the Aggregates" (Skandhaka):
some say that the "aggregate" (skandha) refers to offenses, which are the objects of discipline.
The claim that the *pāda* (sections) constitute the practice of remediation is not necessarily so;
for it need not be asked whether the *pāda* and *skandha* (aggregates) both invariably contain these two meanings.
One must not be biased or fixed in one direction. Second, regarding the classification of those belonging to the Bodhisattva Vehicle:
within this, there are first the chapters and secondly the sections;
there are two distinct types of chapters.
That is to say, there are four offenses within the first category: *pārājika* and *dukkaṭa*.
The first arises from being moved by greed to praise oneself and disparage others with one's own mouth.
Therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"For the sake of craving gain and profit,
a bodhisattva praises his own virtues and disparages others."
This is called the first *pārājika* rule.
Second, due to stinginess, one does not move body or speech.
Thus, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
Because the bodhisattva is by nature stingy and parsimonious,
when suffering beings who have no one to rely upon come to him seeking what they love, he fails to give rise to a compassionate heart to bestow what they seek.
If one, desiring to hear the Dharma, is stingy and refuses to speak it,
this is called the second *pārājika* offense.
Third, due to malice, one agitates body and speech.
Therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"If a bodhisattva, out of anger, utters harsh and evil words and their intent still does not cease,
they further strike with their hands or inflict blows with sticks or stones."
Violence, terror, and hatred increase to such an extent that when an offender seeks repentance, they do not accept the confession; instead,
they harbor resentment and refuse to let it go.
This is called the third *pārājika* offense.
Fourth, due to delusion, one establishes a counterfeit [teaching] and slanders the true Dharma.
Thus, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
When a bodhisattva slanders the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and zealously establishes counterfeit teachings,
this is called the fourth *pārājika* offense.
Within the second section, there is a distinction based on the differing causes that give rise to these offenses.
That is to say, the medium and inferior grades.
Next, the meaning of "accumulation" (skandha) is analyzed:
as for the meaning of accumulation, it is singular in terms of its name.
There are three ways of explaining its meaning:
first, by dividing it into three according to the three categories of the remedial precepts (*pratipakṣa-śīla*);
second, by dividing it into three according to the differences in their respective causes.
Therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"If a bodhisattva commits an offense involving a pārājika matter due to predominant afflictions,
they lose the bodhisattva ethical discipline."
One should receive it again.
If one commits an offense involving a *pārājika* matter due to middling afflictions,
one should go before three persons.
If one commits an offense beyond that, it is to be confessed as a *duṣkṛta*.
If one commits a transgression involving the afflictions that constitutes a *pārājika* offense,
one must confess it before a single person.
Third, regarding the different categories of offenses committed, there are three:
namely, *pārājika*, *sthūlātyaya*, and *duṣkṛta*.
The first and the third are as explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
Regarding the *sthūlātyaya* offenses, they are as discussed within the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* concerning the heterodox and the orthodox.
Fourth, regarding the general classification, there is a fourfold analysis:
first, the analysis of cessation and performance.
1. The classification of the two types of karma;
2. The differences in the obstacles; 3.
The distinctions in the remedies. First, regarding the cessation of the agent:
In the Śrāvaka Dharma, as in the first section, there is only the commission of an offense (*āpatti*);
in the remaining sections, both abstention and commission apply.
Although there is abstention from an offense, it is established for the purpose of completing the commission of an offense through the maintenance of abstention (*vairamaṇī-saṃvara*).
In the Bodhisattva precepts, both abstention (*saṃvara*) and action (*pravṛtti*) may constitute transgressions.

For example, while the ethical discipline of restraint (*śīla-saṃvara*) and so forth pertain to both abstention and action, the practices of gathering wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*) and gathering sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*) involve only abstention from what is to be countered, not the performance of action.
In order to establish transgressions as observances, the second [section] is the differentiation of the three types of action (*trikarma*).
Within the Śrāvaka Dharma, this primarily takes up the two actions of body and speech,
while also including the mental states that serve as the means for initiating action and the intention regarding the timing of the action.
As it is said, "With what kind of mind, etc.?
the greedy minds and so forth arising from right action are not subsumed under the *pārājika* or *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses;
in the Bodhisattva Dharma, one passes through all three types of action.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"The mental ground of a bodhisattva possesses faults,
namely the seven types of vitarka and vicāra, and so forth."
For the śrāvakas, however, this is not the case.

Regarding the relationship between that which is to be remedied and its remedy, the meaning is as explained in the chapter on the three clusters of precepts (*tri-skandha-śīla*). Third, regarding the differences in what is obstructed:
The quality of severing the obstacles to the Dharma of the śrāvakas;
the three qualities regarding the obstacles to the Dharma of the bodhisattvas;
and the quality of severing the obstacles governed by the restraint of discipline.

The wisdom-virtue is comprised of that which is opposed by the obstacles to the gathering of what is wholesome; the beneficence-virtue is comprised of that which is opposed by the obstacles to the gathering of sentient beings.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
The morality of restraint is the cause for the quality of abandonment;
the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas is the cause for the quality of wisdom;
the morality of gathering sentient beings is the cause for the quality of beneficence.
Since only this can serve as the antidote, we know that the obstacles it counteracts are distinct.
Regarding the fourth distinction of the antidotes,
the Dharma of the Śrāvakas is first explained.
Next, the Dharma of Bodhisattvas and the Dharma of Śrāvakas are discussed;
first, these two are distinguished by contrasting them with respect to the Bodhisattva.
Second, regarding the specific explanation of the antidotes for the śrāvakas, there are both general and specific aspects.
The first is explained generally as follows:
it merely suppresses and subdues [the afflictions] but does not eradicate the offenses.
There are two distinctions in its essence:
first, to weaken [the afflictions] by observing their already arisen disintegration and subduing them;
this is the antidote of relinquishment.
Second, regarding the cause that gives rise to offenses when one has not yet initiated contemplation:
by abandoning that cause, one ensures that the karmic fruit does not arise.
Second, the remedies do not exceed two types.
There are two types: the general and the specific.
The meaning of the specific is as explained in the sequence of the preceding five chapters.
The distinctions within the general meaning are sevenfold.
First, the mutual disclosure that interrupts the continuity;
this refers to cases where what has already arisen is compared with what has already arisen, encompassing both the five categories (*pañcāpatti*) and the seven groups (*saptasaṃghāvaśeṣa*).
Second, the imposition of the disciplinary penalty of *śikṣādattaka*.
This refers to the first two categories of offenses for which an antidote has already arisen;
as for the remainder, they cannot be remedied by the Sangha.
Question:
If that is so, why does the Vinaya state:
"Four matters are beyond remedy;
thirteen are remediable"?
As for the others, they are not rescued out of order. Answer:
This refers to those whose minds are free from heavy remorse; if one were to say it is a remedy for the first category [of offenses], [it would be incorrect].
If this person commits [an offense] without a single thought of concealment and gives rise to profound remorse, they may perform the *pārājika* repentance throughout their entire life.

This is because these three were not originally prohibited but were later permitted; from the perspective of the ninety-one [minor offenses] and beyond, they are prohibitory offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) rather than natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
The fourth is abandonment;
this is the lightest among the seventh category of the fifth section.
The fifth is transformation, excluding the first section.
Regarding the first category, which applies generally to the others:
there are six ways in which the causes and conditions for the arising of offenses are observed as they truly are.
This applies generally to all [offenses], whether in relation to the five categories (*pañcāpatti*) or the seven groups (*saptasaṃghāvaśeṣa*).
If one expects [the offenses] that have already arisen, they subsequently fall under the four categories and six groups;
the seventh is obtained through the nature of things (dharmatā).
Generally speaking, they fall under the five categories and seven groups.
These points are as clarified in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and as explained in the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*).
Next, regarding the differentiation of the bodhisattva-dharmas:
First, the counteractive of suppression;

second, the counteractive of eradication. Regarding the first, it shall be discussed by way of the aggregates (*skandha*). Although the first aggregate is not explicitly mentioned in the text, [it is to be understood as follows].
The remedial methods may be understood by analogy.
The second group [of offenses] involves three persons;
if there are more than three, the method of confession is as it is for the Śrāvakas.
Therefore, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
"If one commits an offense against the *pārājika* dharmas due to middling afflictions,
one should confess before three persons."
If one exceeds three people, one should kneel with palms joined and perform a *duṣkṛta* confession.
If the affliction is of a minor grade, whether in the presence of another person or not,
one should give rise to a pure mind and vow not to commit the offense again.
Therefore, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
"If one commits an offense of the *pārājika* category due to the underlying afflictions, or commits any other offense,
one should confess it before a single person."
If there is no person who is like the Dharma, one should give rise to a pure mind and think:
"I shall never again commit this offense."
In future lives, one should constantly maintain the vows of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*).
If one can do so, whatever transgressions have been committed will be eliminated.
Second is the remedy of elimination (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*).
Contemplate that offenses have no intrinsic nature.
Thus, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
"One should eliminate them; do not disturb the mind."
The transgression is neither within, nor without, nor in between.
